title: Fire Marshal's Office: operational permits and inspections for a glass studio (hot work, compressed gases, LP-gas, industrial ovens, open flames, assembly)
question: My glass studio uses a gas furnace, glory hole, kilns, torches, oxygen and propane, and I may host events. What does the Charlottesville Fire Marshal's Office require, which Statewide Fire Prevention Code permits apply, and what do they cost?
office: Charlottesville Fire Department, Fire Marshal's Office (Community Risk Reduction); the City's fire official under the Statewide Fire Prevention Code
summary: Virginia's Statewide Fire Prevention Code (SFPC, 13VAC5-52) governs how a glass studio stores and uses fuel gases, oxygen and open flames once it is open; Charlottesville enforces it through the Fire Marshal's Office (434-970-3328) under the Charlottesville Fire Prevention and Protection Code (City Code ch. 12), which may be more restrictive than the state code. SFPC § 107.2 lets the fire official require operational permits from Table 107.2, which the locality fills in. The table rows that fit a hot shop are: hot work (fixed-site hot work equipment and portable hot work equipment used inside a structure, and public exhibitions or demonstrations where hot work is conducted); compressed gas above 504 cubic feet of oxidizing gas (oxygen) or 200 cubic feet of flammable gas; LP-gas storage and use; industrial ovens regulated by Chapter 30; open flames and candles in assembly or dining areas; places of assembly; and commercial cooking for a cafe. The City does not publish which of these it requires, its application forms, or a fire-permit fee schedule, so the first step is to call the Fire Marshal's Office with the equipment and gas list before the building permits are final. Permits are applied for on the fire official's forms, issued after inspection, kept on the premises, lapse if the activity does not start within six months, and are not transferable. Fire protection systems (sprinklers, alarms, hood suppression) must be inspected, tested and maintained and the contractor's reports uploaded to the City's web-based vendor (IROL, $18.99 per report, paid by the contractor) within 30 days. Decisions of the fire official are appealed first to the local board of appeals, then to the State Building Code Technical Review Board.

legal_basis.quote: The Fire Prevention Code shall supersede fire prevention regulations heretofore adopted by local governments or other political subdivisions. Local governments are hereby empowered to adopt fire prevention regulations that are more restrictive or more extensive in scope than the Fire Prevention Code provided such regulations do not affect the manner of construction, or materials to be used in the erection, alteration, repair, or use of a building or structure

Any local government may enforce the Fire Prevention Code in its entirety or with respect only to those provisions of the Fire Prevention Code relating to open burning, fire lanes, fireworks, and hazardous materials.
Appeals concerning the application of the Code by the local enforcing agency shall first lie to a local board of appeals and then to the State Building Code Technical Review Board.

A schedule of such costs shall be adopted by the local governing body in a local ordinance. A locality shall not charge an overtime rate for inspections conducted during the normal business hours established by the locality.

The fire official may require notification prior to (i) activities involving the handling, storage, or use of substances, materials, or devices regulated by the SFPC; (ii) conducting processes that produce conditions hazardous to life or property; or (iii) establishing a place of assembly.

Operational permits may be required by the fire official as permitted under the SFPC in accordance with Table 107.2, except that the fire official shall require permits for the manufacturing, storage, handling, use, and sale of explosives.
2. Use of portable hot work equipment inside a structure.
3. Fixed-site hot work equipment such as welding booths.
1. Public exhibitions and demonstrations where hot work is conducted.
When approved, the fire official shall issue a permit to carry out a Hot Work Program. This program allows approved personnel to regulate their facility's hot work operations.
An operational permit is required for the storage, use, or handling at normal temperature and pressure (NTP) of compressed gases in excess of the amounts listed in this table.

legal_basis.citation: 13VAC5-52-70 (SFPC Table 107.2, Permit Amounts for Compressed Gases: Oxidizing)
legal_basis.quote: Oxidizing (including oxygen)

legal_basis.citation: 13VAC5-52-70 (SFPC Table 107.2, Permit Amounts for Compressed Gases: Flammable)
legal_basis.quote: Flammable (except cryogenic fluids and liquefied petroleum gases)

Exception: An operational permit is not required for individual containers with a 500-gallon (1893 L) water capacity or less or multiple container systems having an aggregate quantity not exceeding 500 gallons (1893 L), serving occupancies in Group R-3.
Industrial ovens. An operational permit is required for operation of industrial ovens regulated by Chapter 30.
Open flames and candles. An operational permit is required to use open flames or candles in connection with assembly areas or dining areas of restaurants or drinking establishments.
Places of assembly. An operational permit is required to operate a place of assembly.
Commercial cooking. An operational permit is required for the operation of commercial cooking appliances in occupancies other than assembly occupancies or dwellings.
Application for a permit shall be made on forms prescribed by the fire official.

Before a permit is issued, the fire official shall make such inspections or tests as are necessary to ensure that the use and activities for which application is made comply with the provisions of this code.
Permits shall remain in effect until revoked or for such period as specified on the permit. Permits are not transferable.
Issued permits shall be kept on the premises designated therein at all times and shall be readily available for inspection by the fire official.

A permit shall become invalid if the authorized activity is not commenced within six months after issuance of the permit or if the authorized activity is suspended or abandoned for a period of six months after the time of commencement.

The local governing body may establish a fee schedule. The schedule shall incorporate unit rates, which may be based on square footage, cubic footage, estimated cost of inspection, or other appropriate criteria.
A permit shall not be issued until the designated fees have been paid.

steps.step: Call the Fire Marshal's Office early with the equipment and gas list
steps.how: The City publishes no list of the Table 107.2 operational permits it requires, no forms and no fire-permit fee schedule, and the Fire Marshal page itself is about home fire safety. SFPC § 107.1 lets the fire official require prior notification of processes that produce hazardous conditions and of establishing a place of assembly, so call before the building permit plans are final. Have ready: the furnace and glory hole fuel (city natural gas or propane) and Btu input; kiln types; torch gases (oxygen, propane, natural gas) and the number and size of cylinders or tanks on site; whether propane will be stored outdoors in a tank; the occupant load for classes and events; and whether there will be a cafe with cooking. Ask which permits, which inspections, the fee and whether a Hot Work Program permit (which lets trained staff authorize their own hot work) is available.
steps.deadline: Before fuel-gas and equipment plans are finalized; SFPC permits must be in hand before the activity starts

steps.step: Identify the operational permits that fit a hot shop under SFPC Table 107.2
steps.who: Operator; the fire official decides which it requires
steps.how: Hot work: a permit is required for fixed-site hot work equipment, for portable hot work equipment used inside a structure (except work under a construction permit), and for public exhibitions and demonstrations where hot work is conducted, which covers public classes and sip-and-blow events. Compressed gas: a permit is required above 504 cubic feet (NTP) of oxidizing gas including oxygen, 200 cubic feet of flammable gas, and 6,000 cubic feet of inert gas; a single large oxygen cylinder or a cylinder bank can exceed 504 cubic feet. LP-gas: a permit is required for storage and use of LP-gas; the exemption for containers up to 500 gallons applies only to Group R-3 homes, so propane at a studio needs one. Industrial ovens: a permit is required to operate industrial ovens regulated by Chapter 30 (Chapter 30 of the fire code covers fuel-fired and electric ovens and furnaces; whether the fire official treats a glass furnace or kiln as one is a question to ask). Open flames and candles: a permit is required for open flames in assembly areas or dining areas of restaurants or drinking establishments. Places of assembly: a permit is required to operate one. Commercial cooking: a permit is required for commercial cooking appliances in non-assembly, non-dwelling occupancies (a cafe kitchen). Cutting and welding also needs a permit if cold-working includes it.
steps.quote: Operational permits may be required by the fire official as permitted under the SFPC in accordance with Table 107.2, except that the fire official shall require permits for the manufacturing, storage, handling, use, and sale of explosives.

steps.step: Apply on the fire official's forms and pay the fee
steps.how: Applications are made on forms prescribed by the fire official; Charlottesville posts none, so request them from the Fire Marshal's Office. Under § 27-98 the City may charge fees to defray the cost of enforcement, set by ordinance in a schedule of costs; the SFPC adds that a local fee schedule must use unit rates and that no permit issues until the fee is paid. No fire-permit fee appears in the NDS Fee Schedule read for this file. Ask the office for the City Code ch. 12 fee schedule.
steps.fee: Set by City ordinance under Va. Code § 27-98 and SFPC § 107.13; not published on the pages read
steps.quote: Application for a permit shall be made on forms prescribed by the fire official.

steps.step: Pass the fire official's inspection before the permit is issued
steps.how: The fire official makes the inspections or tests needed to confirm the use and activities comply with the code before issuing a permit. Expect checks on cylinder storage and securing, separation of oxygen from fuel gases, propane tank siting and protection, clearances around furnaces and glory holes, fire extinguishers, exits and occupant load for classes and events, and any hood suppression in a cafe kitchen. The Fire Marshal's Office lists restaurants, assembly and event spaces, high-hazard buildings, breweries and distilleries and multi-use commercial buildings among the occupancies it inspects.
steps.quote: Before a permit is issued, the fire official shall make such inspections or tests as are necessary to ensure that the use and activities for which application is made comply with the provisions of this code.

steps.step: Keep the permits on the premises and keep them alive
steps.how: Issued permits stay on the premises, readily available to the fire official. A permit becomes invalid if the activity does not start within six months of issuance or is suspended for six months. Permits are not transferable, so a change of owner needs new ones. Permits run until revoked or for the period written on them; ask whether Charlottesville issues them annually.
steps.deadline: Activity must begin within six months of issuance (SFPC § 107.9)
steps.quote: Issued permits shall be kept on the premises designated therein at all times and shall be readily available for inspection by the fire official.

steps.step: Have fire protection systems inspected, tested and maintained, with reports filed through IROL
steps.who: Operator (property owner keeps the records); certified inspection contractors file the reports
steps.how: City Code § 12-32(11) requires fire protection and life safety systems (sprinklers, fire alarms, kitchen hood suppression, extinguishers' larger systems, standpipes) to be inspected, tested and maintained at the intervals the SFPC sets, with itemized records kept on the premises. The contractor who does the work must upload the report to the City's designated web vendor, InspectionReportsOnline.net (IROL), within 30 days; compliant reports within 30 days, deficient ones within five days, and critical ones reported to the Fire Department immediately with the upload within 24 hours. IROL charges the contractor $18.99 per report; it is free to the City and to business owners. Confirm your service providers are registered with IROL. Semi-annual kitchen hood cleaning and annual hood suppression reports are on the list of systems to be submitted.
steps.deadline: Reports within 30 days of the inspection; deficient within five days; critical immediately with upload within 24 hours (IROL page)
steps.fee: $18.99 per report, charged to the contractor
steps.quote: Businesses with fire prevention systems are required to schedule an inspection for these devices. Inspections are completed by a third-party contractor and submitted on their behalf to CFD through the IROL system.

steps.step: For events and tents: fire inspection of tents and the assembly permit
steps.who: Operator; Fire Department; NDS Building Code Office (tent permits)
steps.how: For events on City property the Special Event Regulations say tents over 900 square feet need a permit from the City Building Code Office in NDS, tents between 400 and 900 square feet need no permit but must be inspected by the Fire Department before use, and pop-up canopy tents are not allowed on the Downtown Mall. On the studio's own lot a tent still needs the building-code tent permit where its size requires one (the Building Permit Application has a Tent option; $50 per tent in the fee schedule). An open-flame demonstration at an event is public hot work under Table 107.2, and candles or open flames in an assembly or dining area need the open-flames permit.
steps.fee: Tent permit: $50 per tent (NDS Fee Schedule, 'Tent Fee - Temporary')
steps.quote: Tents greater than 400 sq. ft. but less than 900 sq. ft. do not require a permit, but

caveats: The City of Charlottesville publishes no fire operational-permit list, application form or fee schedule on charlottesville.gov. The Fire Marshal page covers home fire safety and gives one phone number. Which Table 107.2 permits the City requires, how much they cost, how long they run and how to apply can only be settled by calling 434-970-3328.

City Code chapter 12 (Charlottesville Fire Prevention and Protection Code) is quoted only as the Fire Department's Third Party Inspections page reproduces § 12-32(11). The rest of chapter 12, including any local amendments and the fee ordinance, sits on Municode and was not read because Municode's terms forbid reprinting.

The Table 107.2 rows are quoted from 13VAC5-52-70 (the 2021 SFPC as amended). Whether a glass furnace, glory hole or kiln is an 'industrial oven regulated by Chapter 30' is an interpretation for the fire official; Chapter 30 of the SFPC was not read.

Compressed-gas thresholds (oxygen 504 cubic feet, flammable 200 cubic feet, inert 6,000 cubic feet at NTP) are per the permit-amounts table; cylinder contents vary by size, so compare your supplier's cylinder volumes against them.
The building-code side (fuel-gas piping, hoods, clearances, occupancy classification) is in glass_studio_building_mechanical; the construction permit and the operational permit are separate.
The appeal section of the SFPC (13VAC5-52, Section 112) was not read; deadlines are stated only as the statute frames them.
